title: Mend the Harness
premise: Find a cracked trace while harnessing behind the Western Hotel, take the leather to the saddler and the iron to the smith at Lake and Canal, and decide at the Green Tree whether the outfit is fit for the road.

opening.text:
JAUNT: MEND THE HARNESS. Sunset in the wagon yard behind the Western Hotel, and you leave on the long road west at first light. The teams in this yard outnumber the guests. While you harness up for a trial turn, the near trace shows a crack by the buckle.

Two trades mend an outfit: the saddler sees to leather and the smith to iron. Both came to Chicago in 1833, the year immigration 'assumed proportions surpassing all expectation', and both keep shop at the same crossing. Find the trouble, get it fixed before dark, and decide over supper at the Green Tree whether the outfit is fit for the road.

stops.text: Behind W. H. Stow's Western Hotel at Randolph and Canal stands a large stable and the yard the wagon trains drive into, with entrances from both streets. Stow's account calls it one of the most important parts of the house, for the teams were as numerous as the guests. Under the county's 1831 tariff a horse kept all night cost 50 cents and a feed 25: a team is not cheap to stand idle.
stops.narrative: The near trace is cracked by the buckle. Look further?

choices.label: Go over every strap, buckle and hook
choices.consequence: The trace is cracked, and the iron hook it fastens to on the whiffletree is worn thin.

choices.label: Unbuckle the cracked trace and go
choices.consequence: One strap off the harness. Nothing else is looked at.

stops.text: Up Canal to Lake Street. Goss & Cobb opened a saddle and harness shop at this corner in 1833, promising that repairing would be immediately attended to when brought to their shop. Silas B. Cobb was one of that year's arrivals. The partners parted in February 1835, and Cobb's June card says he will carry on alone. Tonight, as every night, there are traces waiting.
stops.narrative: Leave the trace for the saddler, or bind it yourself?

choices.label: Leave the trace to be restitched
choices.consequence: Leather work, the repairing the card promises. The trace comes back sound.

choices.label: Bind the crack with twine yourself
choices.consequence: It will hold for a short run, not for a long road.

stops.text: Leather is the saddler's; iron is the smith's. On the same crossing Asahel Pierce, another arrival of 1833, began a blacksmith shop in October that year, and Andreas records him doing the ironing for the first stage line between Chicago and St Louis in January 1834. A man who irons the St Louis stage can make one worn hook sound.
stops.narrative: Is there iron to see to?

choices.label: Leave the worn hook for the forge
choices.consequence: Iron work, not leather. The whiffletree hook is made sound.

stops.text: East along Lake to West Water and the Green Tree, which James Kinzie built in 1833 as the first house in the place put up for hotel purposes, 'so called from an oak tree standing close by'. Old settlers recalled Chester Ingersoll keeping it from 1834 to 1837. It will outlast nearly everything in sight: moved in 1880, it still stood in 1895, 'the oldest memento of early taverns'.
stops.narrative: Ready for the long road, or a short run tomorrow?

choices.label: Call the outfit ready for the road
Keep tomorrow's trip short
choices.consequence: Somewhere near town, and back by dark.

legs.note: Out of the yard and a block north on Canal Street to Lake.
legs.story: The cracked trace rides on the seat beside you.

legs.note: A few steps along the same crossing.
East along Lake Street to West Water, on the west bank of the South Branch.

endings.text: A short run near town tomorrow, then, and the long road another day. Whatever was left unchecked or only bound with twine will be tested close to help. Careful is not quite ready, but it is not reckless either.

Leather to the saddler and iron to the smith: the trace restitched, the whiffletree hook made sound, and every strap and buckle looked over before dark. At first light the outfit takes the long road, fit for whatever the prairie throws at it.

The trace is sound again, but you found the worn hook and drove past the forge with it. The leather will hold on the long road; whether the iron will is a question for the first hard pull, a long way from Asahel Pierce.
The trace is restitched and the outfit takes the long road. Nobody looked at the iron, so nobody knows the whiffletree hook is worn thin. Sound leather, untried iron: next time, look over everything.

keepsake.title: Sound Tack
keepsake.text: A fictional note of one harness check: a cracked trace, a worn hook, and what was done about each. No real repair, charge or customer of either shop is written on it.

evidence.text: W. H. Stow's account of his Western Hotel at Randolph and Canal puts a large stable in the rear and a yard the wagon trains were driven into, with entrances from both streets, and calls it one of the most important parts of the house, for the teams were as numerous as the guests.
evidence.locator: chicagology pre-fire page 278, Town of Chicago: W. H. Stow's account of the Western Hotel ('In the rear was the large stable and the yard into which the trains were driven').

evidence.text: The stable is placed in the scene south of the hotel, across the yard, because the source places it only 'in the rear' of a house that fronts north onto Randolph; its fabric is described by no source.
evidence.reasoning: Follows the structure record western_hotel_stable, whose position is inferred against the hotel's own facade bearing and whose construction, height and door are all inferred. The stop speaks of the stable and the yard as the source does and describes nothing of the building itself.

evidence.text: Goss & Cobb advertised that they had opened a saddle and harness shop on the corner of Lake and Canal streets, making saddles, harness, bridles, martingales and trunks to order, and that repairing would be immediately attended to when brought to their shop.
evidence.locator: 26 Nov 1833 (Vol. I No. 1), p. 3, col. 4, the advertisement headed 'Saddle & Harness Making' (extracted claim chicago_democrat_1833_11_26#c019), read from the scan; the full reading is on the structure record goss_cobb_saddlery.

evidence.text: The Goss & Cobb partnership was dissolved on 18 February 1835, and S. B. Cobb's card printed beside the notice says he will continue the business at his shop.
evidence.locator: 13 June 1835, p. 3, col. 6: dissolution notice dated 'Chicago, Feb. 18, 1835' (extracted claim chicago_american_1835_06_13#c015) and Cobb's continuation card (chicago_american_1835_06_13#c016). Transcription-mediated reading, checked against the structure record's reading of the page.

evidence.text: That Cobb's 1835 shop is the 1833 shop at Lake and Canal is reasoned, and which corner of the crossing it held is not attested.
evidence.reasoning: The American's 1835 cards keep the trade and name Lake Street but never resolve the cross street, so the structure record goss_cobb_saddlery identifies the two shops by argument and places the building on the south-east quadrant as a one-in-three choice. The stop says 'this corner' of the crossing and claims no front door.

evidence.text: Asahel Pierce arrived from Vermont on 8 October 1833 and began building a blacksmith shop on Lake Street at the corner of Canal; in January 1834 he did the ironing for the first stage line between Chicago and St Louis.
evidence.locator: Andreas, scan p. 1161, the Asahel Pierce paragraph (arrival, shop at Lake and Canal, the Temple & Co. stage-line ironing).

evidence.text: On this crossing the leather and the iron of an outfit were two trades in two shops: Cobb's card offers harness, bridles and repairing, and Pierce's recorded work is ironing vehicles and making ploughs.
evidence.reasoning: Read from the two firms' own records as the brief asks: the saddler's advertisement lists leather goods and repairing, and Andreas's account of the smith lists iron work only. That a whiffletree hook would go to the smith rather than the saddler is the ordinary division of the two trades, not a recorded repair.

evidence.text: Pierce's shop is at Lake and Canal, and the corner it is modelled on is not attested.
evidence.reasoning: Andreas gives 'on Lake Street, corner of Canal' and no more; the structure record pierce_blacksmith_shop models the south-east corner and says the choice is not attested. The stop says 'on the same crossing' and claims no door.

evidence.text: James Kinzie built the Green Tree in 1833 as the first building in the place erected for hotel purposes; Chester Ingersoll is given as landlord 1834–1837.
evidence.locator: chicagology pre-fire page 127, Green Tree Tavern: construction and landlords; DRLOIH hotel chronology, Green Tree entry.

evidence.text: In 1831 the county authorities made a tariff of rates 'obligatory upon all inn-keepers': 25 cents for each breakfast and supper, 37½ for dinner, 25 for each horse feed, 50 for keeping a horse all night, 12½ for lodging for men, 25 for half a pint of wine, rum or brandy, 18¾ for gin, and 6¼ for a gill of whiskey.
evidence.locator: p. 560, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 98764-98777 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: Immigration in 1833 'assumed proportions surpassing all expectation'; the year's arrivals included John Dean Caton, Silas B. Cobb, Asahel Pierce and the Rev. Jeremiah Porter, and about 165 frame buildings went up.
evidence.locator: p. 90, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 12227-12245 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: The Green Tree was 'so called from an oak tree standing close by', 'one of the most noted in those early days'; it stood until 1880, when it was moved to 33-37 Milwaukee Avenue, 'where it still stands, the oldest memento of early taverns'.
evidence.locator: p. 561, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 98792-98820 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected)

evidence.text: The Green Tree's corner is the north-east corner of Lake and West Water, on the west bank of the South Branch, east along Lake Street from the Canal Street crossing.
evidence.reasoning: The structure record green_tree_tavern places the tavern at Lake and West Water on the owner's ruling T-0141 (position inferred); West Water is the west-bank frontage, so the leg from Lake and Canal runs east along Lake.

evidence.text: The four places are exterior stops in the 1 July 1835 scene. No interior, front door, hostler, saddler or smith at work, keeper or customer on the day is claimed.
evidence.reasoning: Uses the structure records' own scene-date phases: the stable belongs to Stow's 1834 hotel, Cobb's continuation card runs in June and July 1835, Pierce's shop is attested from 1833 and enlarged as his business grew, and Ingersoll's tenancy spans 1835. Every position is inferred. The stops speak of what each house or shop did, not of anyone met there.

evidence.text: The wagon, the long road, the cracked trace, the worn whiffletree hook, the inspection, the restitching, the twine, the work at the forge, the decision at the Green Tree, the endings, the timing inputs and the Sound Tack keepsake are invented connective narrative. Neither shop is claimed to have mended this harness or charged for it.
